fields.meaning: As per the rules; scheduled to
examples: At our school, the rule is that only Japanese may be spoken in the classroom.
By law, people under 20 are not allowed to drink alcohol.
In my family, it's customary for all our relatives to get together on January 2.
I'm scheduled to go to a part-time job interview tomorrow.
"I was supposed to meet Mr. Nakamura here at 10, but..."
In this apartment building, garbage must be put out by 8 a.m.
fields.explain:
Used in workplaces, schools, written rules, announcements, and meetings.
With a time/date: shows a fixed schedule and avoids the nuance of a “personal decision”.
Polite form: ～ことになっております; more formal form in formal written language: ～こととなっております.
Not used for personal habits you set for yourself (in that case use ～ことにしている).
Suits verbs of actions/procedures; rarely used directly with adjectives.

• Expresses a rule, custom, or schedule decided by a group/rule/third party, not by a personal decision.
• Main meaning: “the rule is that…”, “it has been arranged that…”, “it is set that…”.
• Often used for internal rules, regulations, work procedures, meeting schedules, class schedules, flight schedules…
• “Objective/passive” nuance: the speaker only reports an existing rule and cannot change it at will.
• Different from ～ことにしている (a decision set by oneself/a small group).
• Present tense ことになっている implies a rule currently in effect; past ことになった emphasizes “has just been decided”.
fields.notes:
• To emphasize that something has “just” been decided: use the past ことになった; for a rule currently in effect: ことになっている.
• Often used with expressions indicating the source of the rule: 規則で／社内規定で／契約上／法律で + ～ことになっている.
• In service announcements, it can be shortened: ～のみとなっております (only…).
• The logical subject is an organization/rule, but it is usually omitted and a subjectless form is used.
mistakes: Confusing it with ～ことにしている: for self-imposed habits, ～ことになっている is not used.
Using an adjective directly: incorrect. Switch to a verb/rule: 価格は毎年見直すことになっている.
Forgetting the appropriate tense: to express “it has been decided” but not yet in effect now, use ことになった, not ことになっている.
Attributing personal volition: “明日は休むことになっている” follows a schedule/rule, not “I decided it myself”.

examples: "There's plenty of time, so there's no need to hurry like that."
"It's his treat, so I don't think you need to pay."
"There's no need to be so disappointed. You still have a chance."
There's no need to worry. I've prepared properly.
There's no need to rush. Let's proceed as planned.
That problem can be solved right away. There's no need to cry.
fields.explain:
Usually follows the dictionary form of a verb. In conversation, よ/ですよ can be added to soften the sentence.
Reassuring, objective nuance; suits announcements/instructions:提出は今日でなくてもいい →今日出す ことはない。
With the meaning “never”, the subject must be a habit/characteristic:彼は遅刻することはない。

• Used to reassure/advise: “there is no need to …”. More objective nuance than ～なくてもいい, more formal in written language.
• Can also express a habit with strong negation: “I never …”. Requires a context of habit/general behavior.
• Not used to say “should not” (moral warning) → use ～べきではない.
fields.notes:
1) Easy to misread as “there is no such thing/it does not exist”.
→ ～ことはない here means “there is no need/it is not necessary to…”, used to advise or reassure.
2) Often used in conversation, with a light nuance.
→ The meaning is close to “no need to…”.
3) Not used to deny the existence of something.
→ If you want to say “that does not happen”, use a different expression.
mistakes: Confusing it with “should not”: ×遅刻することはない → this means “never late”, not “should not be late”. “Should not” must be 遅刻すべきではない。
Wrong tense: this pattern uses the present; for the past → express it through context: 昨日は急ぐ必要がなかった (～ことはなかった is not used).
Lack of context leads to ambiguity between “no need” and “never”; the JLPT signals it with reassuring keywords (心配/焦る/慌てる) → read it as “no need”.

fields.connection: Aい (drop い) + さ / Na + さ
examples: I toured the factory and was amazed by how advanced the technology was.
With this coat, I won't have to worry about the winter cold either.
The height of this mountain is beyond what I imagined.
I'm feeling how difficult Japanese is.
I was saved by her kindness.
The convenience of the city and the quiet of the countryside: both are hard to give up.
fields.explain:
Used as a noun: takes particles が・は・を・の…, serves as a subject/modifier.
Often comes with a measurement or standard of comparison:高さ3メートル,速さを競う.
With emotions:嬉しさ/悲しさ exist, but when emphasizing the “feeling”, ～み is often more natural.
Neutral style; can be used both in academic/technical contexts (重さ,長さ) and in everyday life (大切さ, ありがたさ).

• Turns an adjective into an abstract noun indicating degree, quality, or attribute: “degree of…/…-ness”.
• Objective nuance, measurable or comparable: 高さ（height）, 速さ（speed）, 大きさ（size）.
• With な形容詞: expresses “…-ness/degree of …”: 静かさ, 便利さ, 真面目さ.
• Distinguish it from ～み: ～さ leans toward the objective/measurable; ～み leans toward feeling/the subjective (詳しく in section 5).
• Often combines with nouns of measurement and standards: 強さ, 弱さ, 深さ, 重さ, 明るさ, 厳しさ.
fields.notes:
• Many four-kanji words become measurement nouns with ～さ: 深さ, 厚さ, 硬さ, 明るさ… very common in JLPT exams.
• 一番＋～さ: used for superlatives together with nominalization, e.g.: この川は深さが一番だ。
• Not every い形容詞 sounds natural with ～さ; if it feels forced, consider another expression (～み/～性/抽象名詞).
mistakes: Confusing it with ～み: “objective vs. subjective”. Example: 誤）その店の安み → More natural: 安さ.
Using ～さ with an unsuitable adjective: 可能さ（可能性 is usually used instead）.
Forgetting the irregular forms: いい→よさ, ない→なさ.
Mechanically translating everything as “-ness” sounds stiff. Be flexible: 高さ=height, 大きさ=size, 便利さ=convenience.

examples: This child is already 6, but still can't even read their own name.
My daughter went ahead and decided to study abroad without even talking to her parents.
Even Sato, a top student, couldn't solve this problem.
"Even I, who am bad at sports, learned to swim in a week, so you'll be fine in three days."
The wife didn't even know how much her husband's salary was.
No matter how much I asked, Mr. Noguchi wouldn't even meet me.
fields.explain:
Used to emphasize an extreme exception, causing surprise.
In ～さえ～ば, さえ marks the “minimum condition”; this form appears very often in the JLPT.
With が/を: usually dropped, and さえ attaches directly after the noun. With に/で/から/へ: keep the particle + さえ.
Style: さえ is neutral; ですら is formal/written language; でも is lighter.

• Meaning 1: Emphasizes the degree “even” with an extreme example → emphasizes surprise, something unexpected.
• Meaning 2: The sufficient-condition pattern ～さえ～ば “as long as … , …” → identifies the minimum condition to achieve a goal.
• Position: さえ attaches right after the emphasized element (noun/case particle; with verbs use Vます＋さえすれば).
• Stronger nuance than でも; ですら is more formal than さえ.
fields.notes:
1) Easily confused with ～まで.
→ ～さえ means “even…”, emphasizing something unexpected; it is not a limit “up to the point of”.
2) Easily confused with ～しか.
→ ～さえ: addition (even… also…).
→ ～しか: limitation, always used with a negative.
3) In the conditional form (～さえ…ば), the meaning is different.
→ ～さえ…ば usually means “as long as… then…”; look carefully at the structure.
explain: ◎ By giving an extreme example, shows that things other than the given example are a matter of course. Can also be replaced with ｢～でも｣.
examples: 1. 小学生でさえ簡単に答えられる問題を間違えてしまった。
I got wrong a question that even elementary school students can answer easily.
2. 世の中には、医者でさえ原因がわからない病気がたくさんある。
There are many diseases in the world whose cause even doctors don't know.
meaning_vi: Even, to the point of
explain: Used to show something of an especially high/low degree that certainly can / cannot be done.
examples: 1. ひらがなさえ書けないんですから、漢字なんて書けません。
I can't even write hiragana, so there's no way I can write something like kanji.
2. そんなこと、子どもでさえ知っている。
Even children know that kind of thing.
mistakes: Wrong position of さえ: it must come right after the emphasized element. 誤）さえ彼に → 正）彼にさえ.
Confusing さえ with だけ: さえ means “even”, だけ means “only”. Their meanings are opposite in many contexts.
Forgetting to drop が/を: 誤）彼をさえ → 彼さえ is usually used.
Confusing ～さえ～ば with ～だけで: both mean “all it takes is”, but ～さえ～ば emphasizes the minimum condition more strongly.

examples: Have no choice but to buy it
You've worked hard to get this far, so you just have to see it through to the end.
I forgot to bring my ticket, so I had no choice but to buy another one at the entrance.
I only have 1,000 yen in cash.
There are only students at the venue.
The trains have stopped, so there's no choice but to walk.
fields.explain:
When expressing a small/insufficient quantity: N/数量＋しかない.
When expressing an unavoidable choice: Vる＋しかない (“have no choice but to …”).
The nuance is often negative/regretful, but it can also be neutral when stating an objective fact.
In spoken language, しかない is more emphatic than だけだ/だけしかない.

• “Only …” with a nuance of strong negation: rules out every other possibility.
• With nouns/quantities: emphasizes a small amount, “only this much”.
• With verbs: “have no choice but to/there is no other way than …”. Carries a sense of reluctance or inevitability.
• Grammatically: しか always goes with a negative predicate (ない). The fixed phrase “～しかない” creates the meaning of obligation.
fields.notes:
• For a polite style: both しかありません/しかないです are acceptable.
• To emphasize scarcity: たった＋数量＋しかない（たった一人しかない）.
• In motivational conversation: “やるしかない！” carries a nuance of determination even though there is no other choice.
examples: 1. ①　野菜しか食べない
Only eat vegetables
2. ②　あの人は肉や魚は食べず、野菜しか食べないそうです。
I hear that person doesn't eat meat or fish, only vegetables.
3. ③　パーティーには二人しか来なかった。
Only two people came to the party.
4. ➃　私のことをこんなにわかってくれるのは、彼女しかいません。
She is the only one who understands me this well.
Variants: ～(より)ほかない・～よりほかしかたがない
mistakes: Forgetting the negative predicate: しか always goes with ない. 誤）お金は千円しか → 正）千円しかない。
Confusing it with だけ: だけ does not carry the nuance of constraint/scarcity and does not need ない.
Using しか alone: a noun/quantity/verb must come before しか.
Redundant double negative: しかない is already negative; do not add ありませんか? in the same clause.

examples: I gave the children two candies each.
Please enter the interview room one at a time, in order.
I memorize ten kanji every day.
It has been getting better little by little.
For this problem, we'll split into three groups and hand out five sheets to each group.
I save 30,000 yen each month.
fields.explain:
Commonly used in instructions, rules, distribution guidelines, or descriptions of progress.
Emphasizes fairness/regularity; for gradual change it is often used with少しずつ/だんだん.
Place ずつ right after the quantity:一つ ずつ （correct）; ×ずつ一つ（wrong order).

• Even distribution: “each …”, “… per person/per item”.
• Little by little: gradual change/progress over time.
• Position: ずつ comes right after the quantity expression it modifies.
fields.notes:
• With decimals/ratios: 0.5杯ずつ（half a cup per person）, 3％ずつ（3％ each time）.
• When saying “little by little” in a long process: 少しずつ＋Vていく／Vてくる is a very natural frame.
• In spoken language, ずつ can be emphasized with ずつでも: 少しずつでも前に進もう。
mistakes: Wrong order: ×ずつ二つ → 二つずつ（correct）.
Dropping the counter when it is needed: ×三ずつ（ambiguous） → 三人ずつ/三個ずつ（clear）.
Confusing it with ごとに: ごとに means “every time/periodically”, not “one per person, one per item”.
The JLPT often tests the position of ずつ in long sentences; rule: always place it right after the quantity phrase it modifies.

fields.connection: Vない (drop ない) + ずに / する → せずに
examples: I overslept this morning and left the house without eating.
It's not good to hope for good results without making an effort.
I went to work without eating breakfast.
He left the room without saying anything.
Since it didn't rain, I didn't have to buy an umbrella.
Walking without looking at your smartphone is dangerous.
fields.explain:
Used to connect a subordinate clause (Vずに、…) placed before the main clause.
More formal than ないで; suits written language/explanations. ないで suits conversation, including commands/requests（～ないでください）.
ずに is not used for direct commands: “Don't …” must use ～ないで（例：撮らないでください）.
With verbs of motion/time, ずに can imply “skipping/jumping over a step”.

• Connects clauses to express that the main action happens while “not doing” action A: “B without A”.
• Emphasizes the absence/exclusion of action A before or at the same time as action B.
• Slightly more formal nuance than ないで; often used in written language, announcements, and essays.
• The fixed pattern ～ずに済む means “get by without having to …/not need to …”.
fields.notes:
• ずに can be chained: 連絡もせずに、謝りもせずに、帰った。
• Reordering clauses to emphasize the main clause: ～ずに、…した（written language often places ずに at the beginning of a sentence）.
• With verbs of perception/social behavior, ずに adds a nuance of impoliteness: 挨拶もせずに去る.
meaning_vi: state of not (=ないで）
explain: ◎ Means "not doing ~". Often used in the form「A (し)ないでBです」when 'not doing (A) as usual but doing (B)'.
examples: 1. 彼は 何も 言わずに 行って しまいました。
He left without saying anything.
2. うちの むすこは よく 考えずに 行動する んです。
My son often acts without thinking.
──────
1. わたしはいつも朝ごはんを食べずに会社へ行く。
I always go to work without eating breakfast.
2. 彼女は何も言わずに部屋を出て行った。
She left the room without saying anything.
3. 「準備体操をせずにプールに入ってはいけません」
「You must not get into the pool without warming up first」
4. 「わたしたちのことを忘れずにいてください」
Please don't forget us. meaning_vi: Not doing something (but doing something else) ⏐ explain: Used when we skip an action that we would naturally, normally do ⏐ examples: 1. 辞書を使わずに書いたので、自信がありません。
I wrote it without using a dictionary, so I'm not confident.
2. 昨夜、歯をみがかずに寝てしまった。
Last night I ended up going to bed without brushing my teeth.
mistakes: Wrong irregular forms: 誤）来りずに×／しずに× → 正）来ずに（こずに）／せずに。
Confusing its role with ないでください: ずに is not used for requests/prohibitions.
Choosing a verb that does not fit “not … but …”, causing a logical contradiction (e.g. 例４ requires a pragmatic reading).
JLPT: often sets traps comparing ずに・ないで・ことなく; pay attention to the formal nuance and the phrase ずに済む.
